entities.name: Library of Alexandria
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Library of Alexandria was the greatest library of the ancient world, founded in the Egyptian city of Alexandria c. 295 BCE under Ptolemy I Soter and expanded under Ptolemy II Philadelphus, with the scholar Demetrius of Phalerum as its first head. At its height, it may have contained 400,000–700,000 scrolls — virtually the entire corpus of known Greek literature, science, philosophy, and much of the knowledge of the ancient Near East, Egypt, and beyond.

The Library was the intellectual engine of the Hellenistic world. Its affiliated scholars included Euclid (geometry), Eratosthenes (who calculated the Earth's circumference to within 2% accuracy), Archimedes (mechanics and mathematics), Aristarchus (who proposed heliocentrism 1,800 years before Copernicus), Herophilus (founder of anatomy), and Callimachus (who created the first systematic catalogue of Greek literature). The Library embodied the Ptolemaic kings' project of collecting all human knowledge — agents were reportedly sent to buy books from ships docking at Alexandria, and copies were made before the originals were returned.

The Library's fate is one of antiquity's most mythologized stories. It was not destroyed in a single catastrophe — the common narrative of Julius Caesar's fire (48 BCE) burning the Library is only one of several incidents of damage. The Library declined gradually through the late Roman period; the Serapeum (annex library) was destroyed in 391 CE during Christian persecution of pagan institutions. The final Arab conquest of Alexandria (641 CE) is sometimes cited as the Library's end, but this too is probably mythologized. The Library represents the ideal of universal knowledge — its symbolic destruction has made it the most powerful image of irretrievable intellectual loss in Western culture.
